strengths: Addresses a genuine practical gap: unadjusted HMC/LMC/MCLMC methods are known to be efficient in high dimensions but lack a principled, automated way to choose step size, which has limited their adoption outside niche fields like lattice QCD and molecular dynamics.

Solid theoretical contribution: the paper derives an exact closed-form relationship (Lemma 4.1) between EEVPD (energy error variance per dimension) and step size for Gaussian targets, and rigorously proves (Theorem 4.2) that EEVPD upper bounds both a covariance-matrix bias metric and squared Wasserstein-2 distance, with careful convexity/monotonicity proofs given in the appendix.

The proposed covariance bias metric b_cov is well-motivated with nice theoretical properties (divergence, basis invariance, connection to effective sample size), and is a sensible, practically useful convergence diagnostic.

Extensive empirical validation: the Gaussian-derived bound is numerically shown to extend reasonably well to a range of non-Gaussian benchmark problems (Rosenbrock, Brownian motion, German Credit, Funnel, Item Response, Stochastic Volatility) for both HMC and MCLMC, lending credibility to the method's practical applicability beyond the theoretical setting.

Comprehensive experimental comparison across adjusted and unadjusted samplers (NUTS, aLMC/uLMC, aMCLMC/uMCLMC) on multiple benchmarks with dimensionality 36-2429, showing consistent advantages for unadjusted methods with automatic tuning, including comparison against grid-searched near-optimal adjusted baselines, which strengthens the practical significance claim.

Good reproducibility support: pseudocode for the tuning algorithm, detailed benchmark descriptions, ablation study on EEVPD sensitivity, and a link to open-source implementation in BlackJax with accompanying benchmarking code.

The illustrative scaling example (Figure 2) and connection to established theoretical dimension-scaling results (Beskos et al. 2013, Durmus and Eberle 2023) provide a clear intuitive motivation grounded in existing literature.
weaknesses: The core theoretical guarantee (Theorem 4.2) is proven only for Gaussian targets; its extension to non-Gaussian problems is only empirically supported and admits known failure cases (e.g., Brownian motion example off by ~1.5x, described in the text), leaving the black-box tuning scheme's reliability on general problems without formal guarantees.

The bias-variance tradeoff heuristic used to set the target EEVPD (Appendix C, 'optimal squared bias should be one fifth of the mean squared error tolerance') is derived only for a 1D standard Gaussian second-moment estimation problem with unadjusted HMC, and it is unclear how well this generalizes to the higher-dimensional, non-Gaussian, and different-functional (e.g., MCLMC) settings used throughout the rest of the paper.

The extension of the EEVPD-based tuning scheme to MCLMC is justified only heuristically ('unadjusted MCLMC has a notion of energy... so we will also test MCLMC') without a corresponding theoretical bound analogous to Theorem 4.2, despite MCLMC being prominently used in the main experimental comparisons.

Some benchmarks (Rosenbrock, Funnel) become numerically unstable at higher step sizes/EEVPD, and it is unclear how the tuning algorithm detects or avoids this instability region in a fully black-box manner without user intervention, which could undermine the claimed hands-off usability.

The paper does not include comparisons against alternative principled approaches to bias control for unadjusted samplers beyond the standard adjusted baselines (NUTS, MALT, aMCLMC), nor does it deeply discuss computational overhead/cost of the EEVPD tuning procedure itself relative to total sampling budget.

Presentation could be improved in places, e.g. dense notation in Section 3-4 and the paper relies heavily on appendices for essential proofs and experimental details, which may hinder readability of the main text in isolation.

The choice of the conservative default EEVPD (3e-4) is somewhat ad hoc and benchmark specific tuning (e.g., Stochastic Volatility requiring much smaller EEVPD) suggests the 'black-box' scheme may still require occasional problem-specific adjustment in practice, partially undercutting the black-box claim.

strengths: Rigorous, fully-proved theoretical result (Theorem 4.2, Appendix B) establishing a closed-form relationship between EEVPD and asymptotic covariance-matrix bias / Wasserstein distance for Gaussian targets, including sharpness conditions.

Addresses a genuine and practically important gap: the lack of a principled, automatic step-size selection scheme for unadjusted HMC/LMC/MCLMC, which currently limits their use outside specialized fields.

Introduces a covariance-error metric (b_cov) with useful theoretical properties (divergence, basis invariance, closed-form relation to effective sample size for Gaussians), which is a nice methodological contribution in its own right.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across several standard Bayesian hierarchical benchmarks (36 to 2429 dimensions), comparing against NUTS, grid-searched adjusted LMC, and adjusted/unadjusted MCLMC, with bootstrap error bars reported.

Illustrative dimension-scaling experiment (Figure 2) clearly demonstrates the practical motivation (d^{1/4} scaling of adjusted vs. constant scaling of unadjusted methods), grounding the paper's premise.
Code/implementation details and benchmark descriptions are provided, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee (Theorem 4.2) is proven only for Gaussian targets; extension to non-Gaussian problems (Section 5) is purely empirical, and the paper itself reports a case (Brownian motion) where the bound is violated by ~1.5x, undermining the 'black-box' and 'rigorously bounds' framing in the abstract.

The key bias-variance tradeoff prescription (Bias^2 = RMSE^2/5, Table 1) is derived from a very narrow toy setting (second moment of a 1D standard Gaussian under HMC in a small-step-size asymptotic limit) yet is applied as a general rule of thumb across all benchmarks without validation of its robustness in higher dimensions or non-Gaussian, non-asymptotic regimes.

The extension of the EEVPD framework to MCLMC is justified only heuristically ('MCLMC has a notion of energy'), without any theoretical backing analogous to Theorem 4.2, despite MCLMC being prominently used in the main experiments.

Comparison design may somewhat favor the proposed method: adjusted LMC is tuned via exhaustive grid search while unadjusted methods use the proposed automatic scheme; although the authors argue this is a stronger baseline, it also means the adjusted baseline was optimized offline in a way not available for a fair 'black-box vs black-box' comparison.

The step-size adaptation algorithm (Algorithm 1, Appendix D.2) includes several heuristic hyperparameters (forgetting factor, log-normal weighting width) that are set by informal experimentation ('we find n=50 to work well') rather than principled derivation or broad sensitivity analysis.

Unadjusted HMC results are omitted from the main experiments ('performance and implementation closely resemble that of LMC'), which is asserted rather than demonstrated, leaving a gap in the empirical validation of the scheme for HMC specifically.

The ablation in Appendix E, while showing some robustness across EEVPD values, also reveals sizable sensitivity for certain problems (e.g., Rosenbrock, Item Response, Stochastic Volatility needing much smaller EEVPD), suggesting the scheme's default recommendation is not universally reliable and problem-specific tuning is still sometimes needed, in tension with the black-box claim.

strengths: Establishes a clean, theoretically grounded link (EEVPD) between the one-step energy error and the asymptotic bias of unadjusted HMC/LMC, with rigorous closed-form bounds for Gaussian targets (Theorem 4.2) that are proven sharp and derived via careful convexity arguments (Appendix B).

Fills a genuine and previously acknowledged gap in the literature: existing theoretical bounds on unadjusted sampler bias (Durmus & Eberle, Bou-Rabee & Eberle, etc.) require global knowledge of the target unavailable in practice, whereas this work turns the theory into a concrete, computable, black-box tuning algorithm.

The proposed EEVPD-targeting scheme is simple to implement online (running variance of one-step energy error) and requires no manual hyperparameter tuning, directly addressing a stated practical barrier to adoption of unadjusted methods in statistics.

Empirical validation is reasonably thorough: the Gaussian theory is numerically confirmed to extend to a range of non-Gaussian benchmarks (Rosenbrock, Brownian motion, German Credit, Funnel) for both HMC and MCLMC, and the derived bias-tolerance-to-EEVPD conversion table (Table 1) is practically useful.

The comprehensive comparison across NUTS, adjusted/unadjusted LMC and MCLMC on realistic hierarchical Bayesian benchmarks (dimensions 36-2429) shows consistent, sizable gains for the proposed unadjusted+auto-tuned approach, including versus grid-search-optimized adjusted baselines, which is a meaningful practical contribution.

Good transparency about limitations: the paper explicitly reports the Brownian motion case where the bound is violated by ~1.5x, notes conservative EEVPD choices, includes an ablation study (Appendix E) showing sensitivity to the EEVPD target, and recommends a standard numerical-analysis validation practice (step-halving) for practitioners.
Reasonable reproducibility: implementation released via BlackJax with code availability noted, and detailed experimental/hyperparameter descriptions in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee (Theorem 4.2) is proven only for Gaussian targets; extension to non-Gaussian targets relies solely on empirical observation across a modest set of benchmarks, with at least one clear counterexample (Brownian motion) where the bound is violated, leaving the generality of the method somewhat unsubstantiated theoretically.

The choice of bias functional (b_cov for second moments, W2 for Lipschitz functions) is somewhat narrow; many Bayesian applications care about tail quantiles, credible intervals, or other functionals not directly covered by these guarantees, and this is not discussed as a limitation.

The heuristic bias-variance tradeoff prescription (Bias^2 = RMSE^2/5, Appendix C) is derived only for a 1D standard Gaussian estimating E[x^2] with HMC; it is unclear how well this generalizes to the higher-dimensional, non-Gaussian, correlated-parameter settings used in the main experiments, and no sensitivity analysis is given for this specific choice (only for EEVPD given a fixed 1/5 ratio).

MCLMC's applicability rests on it having 'a notion of energy' analogous to HMC/LMC, but the same rigorous Gaussian-derived bound is simply assumed to transfer (with an ad hoc adjustment of EEVPD target), which is a heuristic extension rather than a proven result.

Some experimental choices (e.g., using NUTS for preconditioning matrix estimation, grid search only for aLMC and not aHMC, momentum decoherence length chosen via existing literature methods) reduce the fully 'black-box' framing to some degree, since certain hyperparameters/preprocessing steps are not fully automated or justified as generally applicable.

The paper does not compare against alternative adaptive step-size heuristics that might already exist informally in fields like lattice QCD or molecular dynamics, limiting the ability to assess how much of an advance the proposed scheme represents over existing ad hoc practices in domains where unadjusted sampling is already used.

strengths: Establishes a rigorous, closed-form analytic relationship (Theorem 4.2) between the Energy Error Variance Per Dimension (EEVPD) and asymptotic bias (covariance error and Wasserstein distance) for Gaussian targets under unadjusted HMC/LMC, with careful proofs (including convexity lemmas enabling Jensen's inequality bounds).

Addresses a clear and practically important gap: the lack of a principled, automatic step-size selection method for unadjusted samplers, which have been known theoretically to scale better with dimension but were rarely used in practice due to this gap.

Extensive empirical validation across many benchmark problems (Gaussian, Rosenbrock, Funnel, Brownian motion, German Credit, Item Response, Stochastic Volatility) and two large real-world lattice field theory models (over one million dimensions), showing the EEVPD-based tuning is close to grid-search-optimal and that unadjusted methods systematically and substantially outperform adjusted counterparts and NUTS.

The dimensional scaling experiments (Figure 2, Figures 5-6) convincingly illustrate the d^{1/4} cost scaling of adjusted methods versus flat scaling of properly tuned unadjusted methods, supporting the paper's central motivating claim with both idealized and realistic examples.

Thorough treatment of limitations, including an honest discussion of a case (Brownian motion) where the bound is empirically looser than predicted, additional analysis in Appendix C examining sensitivity to tail weight, and practical diagnostic suggestions for detecting when discretization bias might be problematic.

Good reproducibility support: algorithmic pseudocode for the tuning scheme (Appendix E), public implementation in BlackJax, detailed benchmark and model descriptions (Appendix F), and quantified uncertainty via bootstrap (Appendix G.3).
weaknesses: The core theoretical result (Theorem 4.2) is proven only for Gaussian targets; extension to non-Gaussian targets is purely empirical/numerical (Section 5), and the paper acknowledges at least one failure case (Brownian motion) where the bound underestimates bias by ~1.5x, without a full theoretical explanation or general guarantee for practitioners in non-Gaussian settings.

The recommended target EEVPD relies on a heuristic derived from a very specific 1D Gaussian bias-variance analysis (Appendix D, giving the 'bias^2 = RMSE^2/5' rule), whose generality to other functions of interest, higher dimensions, and non-Gaussian posteriors is not rigorously justified beyond empirical spot-checks.

Comparisons to adjusted methods (aLMC via grid search, aMCLMC via fixed acceptance-rate target) and NUTS use different tuning philosophies with different levels of optimization effort; while grid search for aLMC is meant to give it an advantage, this heterogeneity in tuning protocols across methods could make head-to-head efficiency comparisons less clean.

For some higher-dimensional or harder problems (Rosenbrock, Item Response), the fixed conservative EEVPD target used in experiments leads to roughly 2x worse performance than the optimal grid-searched unadjusted step size, suggesting the automatic tuning recipe may leave a non-negligible efficiency gap in some regimes despite claims of near-optimality.

The work focuses on covariance-based (second moment) summary statistics and Wasserstein-bounded Lipschitz functionals; it is unclear how well the method controls bias for other posterior quantities of interest (e.g., quantiles, tail probabilities), an important scope limitation not deeply discussed.

The claim of 'consistently and significantly' outperforming adjusted counterparts is strong; while broadly supported, the actual margins vary substantially by problem (e.g., only modest or no gains on Stochastic Volatility with uLMC vs. aLMC), which slightly tempers the universality of the headline claim.

strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical foundation (Theorem 4.2, with full proofs in Appendix B) relating the Energy Error Variance Per Dimension (EEVPD) to both the covariance-matrix bias and the Wasserstein-2 bias for Gaussian targets under HMC/LMC with a velocity Verlet integrator; the bound is shown to be sharp in the isotropic case.

The core proposed algorithm (adaptive step-size tuning to target a user-specified EEVPD) is simple, essentially free to compute (energy error is a byproduct of gradient evaluation), and directly analogous to acceptance-rate-based dual averaging used for adjusted samplers, making it easy to adopt in practice.

Extensive empirical validation spans synthetic product distributions, standard Bayesian inference benchmarks (Inference Gym models with 36-2429 dimensions), and two real-world lattice field theory problems at over one million dimensions, consistently showing large (up to ~100x) efficiency gains for unadjusted, automatically tuned samplers over adjusted counterparts and NUTS.

The paper is scientifically honest about limitations: it identifies a case (Brownian motion) where the empirical bound is violated by ~1.5x, explores sensitivity to tail weight (Appendix C), and proposes concrete discretization-bias diagnostics analogous to R-hat for initialization bias.

Good reproducibility practices: code is integrated into the public BlackJax library, uncertainty is quantified via bootstrap (Table 4), and an ablation study (Appendix G.2) shows robustness of performance to the exact EEVPD target chosen.
The bias metric b_cov has useful theoretical properties (divergence, effective-sample-size interpretation, basis invariance), which are proven and add rigor to the presentation.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee (Theorem 4.2) is proven only for Gaussian targets; for all non-Gaussian benchmarks the bound is merely observed numerically to often (but not always) hold, and one example (Brownian motion) explicitly violates it by a non-trivial margin (~3% actual bias vs <2% predicted), undermining the claim of a reliable 'automatic' bias-tolerance guarantee for general problems.

The recommended mapping from a target RMSE tolerance to a target EEVPD (Appendix D, bias² = RMSE²/5) is derived from a 1-D Gaussian toy analysis and is used as a general heuristic without rigorous justification for the non-Gaussian, high-dimensional settings where the method is actually deployed.

The proposed step-size tuning algorithm (Appendix E) is presented without any convergence guarantees ('we do not provide any convergence guarantees'), which is a gap given that the paper's main selling point is turning unadjusted MCMC into a principled black-box procedure.

Because the underlying bound can fail silently (as in the Brownian motion case), the paper's practical safety net relies on post-hoc diagnostics (comparing runs at different step sizes) that are optional and not integrated into the automatic procedure itself, somewhat weakening the 'black-box, no manual tuning' framing in the abstract/intro.

Some experimental comparisons are slightly asymmetric: adjusted LMC (aLMC) is tuned via exhaustive grid search to represent a near-optimal baseline, while unadjusted methods use the proposed automatic scheme; although this strengthens the result when unadjusted still wins, it makes the comparison to aLMC not fully apples-to-apples with the black-box framing used for other methods.

HMC is not evaluated at all in the main experiments (Section 7) with justification that it 'closely resembles' LMC, but this claim is not empirically substantiated in the paper, leaving a gap in the otherwise thorough evaluation.

The core algorithmic novelty is relatively modest: the tuning scheme largely reuses standard ideas (dual-averaging-style adaptation, analogous to acceptance-rate tuning) applied to a new but incrementally different target statistic (EEVPD rather than acceptance probability), with the main contribution being the theoretical justification rather than a fundamentally new method.

strengths: Establishes a rigorous, closed-form theoretical relationship (Theorem 4.2, with full proofs in Appendix B) between the Energy Error Variance Per Dimension (EEVPD) and both the covariance-matrix bias and the Wasserstein-2 distance for Gaussian targets, including sharpness conditions and convexity arguments that are carefully proven.

The theory is not left as a purely Gaussian curiosity: Section 5 numerically validates that the same bound holds reasonably well across a broad range of non-Gaussian benchmarks (Rosenbrock, funnel, German Credit, etc.) and even extends to MCLMC, which lacks an exact analytic treatment.

The resulting tuning algorithm fills a genuine, previously acknowledged gap in the unadjusted-sampler literature (no principled black-box step-size selection), and is simple, cheap to compute online, and integrated into a widely used library (BlackJax), aiding reproducibility.

Empirical evaluation is extensive and convincing: multiple standard Bayesian inference benchmarks with grid-search baselines for adjusted samplers (to avoid stacking the deck), bootstrap-based uncertainty quantification (Table 4), and ablations over the EEVPD target (Appendix G.2) showing robustness of the chosen operating point.

Large-scale, realistic, non-product experiments (ϕ⁴ scalar field theory at >10^6 dimensions and U(1) lattice gauge theory at up to 2×10^6 dimensions) demonstrate dramatic, practically meaningful speedups (up to ~100x fewer gradient calls than NUTS) and confirm the constant-cost-with-dimension scaling predicted by the theory/illustrative example.

The paper is transparent about a failure case (Brownian motion, where the bound underestimates bias by ~1.5x) and follows up with additional diagnostics (Appendix C on tail sensitivity) and practical guidance (running half-step-size chains) rather than hiding or glossing over the limitation.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee (Theorem 4.2) is proven only for Gaussian targets; for all non-Gaussian and real-world problems the reliance on the EEVPD-bias relationship is empirical/heuristic, and the paper itself documents at least one benchmark (Brownian motion) where the bound is violated by a non-trivial margin, meaning practitioners cannot know a priori whether the guarantee holds for a novel target.

The recommended target EEVPD value (and the bias/variance 1/5 split) is derived from a small-step-size asymptotic analysis of a 1D standard Gaussian estimating E[x^2] (Appendix D) and then applied broadly by analogy; this heuristic extension to trajectory length, preconditioning, and general multi-dimensional non-Gaussian posteriors is not rigorously justified, only validated post hoc via the ablation in Fig. 9.

The comparison methodology gives grid-search-optimized hyperparameters to adjusted LMC (aLMC) while unadjusted methods use the proposed automatic scheme; although this arguably strengthens the paper's claims (showing black-box unadjusted still wins), it makes some head-to-head efficiency numbers in Tables 1 and 3 not fully apples-to-apples and could be presented with more nuance.

MCLMC's treatment is somewhat informal relative to HMC/LMC: the paper notes MCLMC 'has a notion of energy' allowing the same tuning idea to be applied, but no analytic derivation analogous to Lemma 4.1/Theorem 4.2 is given for MCLMC, so its inclusion in the main large-scale experiments rests entirely on the empirical Section 5 validation.

The discussion of why machine learning applications are omitted ('controversial whether Bayesian neural networks offer any advantage') is a fairly thin justification and leaves open whether the proposed scheme would work well in higher-variance, non-log-concave, or multimodal deep learning posteriors that are increasingly relevant to the ICML audience.
